title: Think like a data engineer
name: Data engineering foundations
description: Understand the people, systems and lifecycle behind useful data.

lessons.title: The data engineering landscape
lessons.objective: Define data engineering and distinguish engineering responsibilities from data science.

sections.title: The core idea
sections.body: Data engineering designs, builds and operates systems that turn raw data into reliable, usable data. Data science often uses that data for analysis and prediction; engineering makes the inputs accessible and dependable.

sections.title: Roles change with context
sections.body: A small team may need one generalist to own ingestion, storage and analytics. A larger organization may separate platform, analytics and infrastructure responsibilities. Data maturity describes how consistently an organization manages and uses its data.

sections.title: Business meets engineering
sections.body: Clarify the decision the data will support, who owns it and when it must arrive. Technical responsibilities include modeling, orchestration, quality, security and operations. A technically impressive pipeline has little value if it misses the business need.

lessons.activity: Choose a campus use case. List its data producers, consumers and one business question.

lessons.title: Follow the data lifecycle
lessons.objective: Trace data from generation to serving and identify lifecycle undercurrents.

sections.title: From source to use
sections.body: Operational applications, devices and external services generate data. Engineers ingest it, choose suitable storage, transform it and serve it to downstream consumers. The wider data lifecycle also includes retention and eventual deletion.

sections.title: Batch or continuous
sections.body: A daily enrollment report can use scheduled batch ingestion. A live service may need streaming updates. Select the arrival pattern from latency and correctness needs rather than tool popularity.

sections.title: The undercurrents
sections.body: Security, data management, DataOps, architecture, orchestration and software engineering span the lifecycle. For example, a change to a source schema can require updates to contracts, tests, permissions and downstream models.

lessons.activity: Draw a source → ingestion → storage → transformation → serving flow. Add quality and ownership checkpoints.

lessons.title: Skills, ownership and trade-offs
lessons.objective: Connect team maturity and responsibilities with practical engineering choices.

sections.title: Start with responsibility
sections.body: For every dataset, identify an owner, consumers, expected freshness and a recovery plan. Ownership helps teams resolve incidents without guessing who should act.

sections.title: Build a balanced skill set
sections.body: SQL, programming and data modeling support implementation. Communication, requirements analysis and prioritization connect those skills to business needs. Operational habits make the system dependable over time.

sections.title: Assess maturity
sections.body: A team using manual exports needs different improvements from a team operating governed, automated pipelines. Choose the next reliable step and document the trade-off.

lessons.activity: Write a dataset contract with its owner, schema, freshness expectation and failure response.

lessons.title: SQL checks, contracts & safe retries
lessons.objective: Turn quality expectations into checks that a pipeline can run.

sections.title: Specify the contract
sections.body: For an orders table, define order_id as a unique non-null key, amount as a non-negative number and event_time as a timestamp. Record the source owner, freshness target and the action to take when a rule fails. A schema check alone cannot tell you whether the values are meaningful.

sections.title: Inspect before publishing
sections.body: Count rows, null keys and duplicate keys before loading the serving table. Compare the row count with a sensible reference window. Quarantine unexpected records for investigation rather than silently discarding them. The thresholds below are illustrative; choose them from your business requirements.

sections.title: Make retries safe
sections.body: A retry may read the same batch twice. Use stable event identifiers and an idempotent merge so the second attempt does not duplicate orders. Store the input partition and completion status, then make backfills explicit. A successful task should mean the expected data was published, not just that a script exited.

lessons.activity: Write three SQL checks for an orders dataset, then explain how your load avoids duplicates when the job retries.
lessons.code:
SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) AS copies
FROM orders
GROUP BY order_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

SELECT COUNT(*) AS missing_keys
FROM orders
WHERE order_id IS NULL;
lessons.codeCaption: Illustrative SQL: a duplicate-key query should return no rows before promotion.

quizzes.question: Which concern spans the entire data engineering lifecycle?
quizzes.explanation: Security and data management affect every stage, from source access to serving and retention.

quizzes.question: Which role most directly owns a dependable ingestion and transformation system?
quizzes.explanation: Data engineers build and operate systems that make data reliably available to consumers.

quizzes.question: A daily report arrives late even though its rows are correct. Which quality concern failed?
quizzes.explanation: Freshness concerns whether data is available within the time window required by its consumers.

quizzes.question: A source sends the same batch twice after a timeout. What helps prevent duplicate output?
options: A random output filename each time
An idempotent load using stable keys
quizzes.explanation: Stable identifiers and idempotent operations let a retry produce the same intended result.

quizzes.question: Which is a business responsibility of a data engineer?
options: Clarifying which decision the data should support
quizzes.explanation: Business context connects technical work to a useful outcome and defines practical service expectations.

quizzes.question: A new column appears upstream. What is the best first response?
options: Automatically treat all values as valid
Evaluate schema compatibility and downstream expectations
quizzes.explanation: A schema change needs to be assessed against contracts and consumers before it is accepted.

quizzes.question: Which activity belongs to the wider data lifecycle?
quizzes.explanation: Data persists beyond transformation and serving; retention and deletion are part of its wider lifecycle.

quizzes.question: Which workload is a reasonable starting point for scheduled batch ingestion?
options: A report required once each morning
quizzes.explanation: Scheduled batch processing can fit daily reporting when the freshness requirement allows it.

quizzes.question: Why document a dataset owner?
options: To make responsibility and incident response clear
To guarantee the data never changes
quizzes.explanation: An owner is accountable for expectations, changes and coordination when issues occur.

quizzes.question: A duplicate-key SQL query returns rows. What should happen before publishing?
options: Ignore the result because the script ran
Investigate or quarantine the duplicates according to the contract
quizzes.explanation: The query identifies a contract violation that needs an explicit response before promotion.

title: Design systems that hold up
name: Data architecture & technology
description: Make architecture decisions around reliability, coupling and business value.

lessons.title: Principles of good architecture
lessons.objective: Connect enterprise goals with data architecture decisions.

sections.title: Architecture has a purpose
sections.body: Enterprise architecture connects business processes and technology. Data architecture describes how data is collected, stored, transformed and used within that larger system.

sections.title: Design for change
sections.body: Prefer clear interfaces, explicit ownership and components that can evolve without forcing every other component to change. Document the assumptions behind each choice.

sections.title: Design for failure
sections.body: Distributed components can fail independently. Plan retries, timeouts, idempotent writes and recovery paths. Reliability is a design concern, not only an operations concern.

lessons.activity: Sketch an architecture for attendance analytics. Annotate one failure mode and its recovery path.

lessons.title: Coupling, services and scale
lessons.objective: Compare monoliths, tiers and microservices in a data system.

sections.title: Coupling creates obligations
sections.body: Tightly coupled components depend on each other's implementation or availability. Loose coupling uses stable interfaces and can reduce the impact of change, but often adds operational complexity.

sections.title: Pick a sensible boundary
sections.body: A monolith may be easier for a small team to build and operate. Services allow independent development and scaling when boundaries and ownership are clear. Neither structure is universally best.

sections.title: Scaling is multidimensional
sections.body: Consider data volume, request rates, latency and the number of independent teams. Partitioning and asynchronous communication help some workloads but introduce consistency and coordination trade-offs.

lessons.activity: Compare a shared-database monolith with event-connected services using cost, reliability and team effort.

lessons.title: Choose technology deliberately
lessons.objective: Evaluate technology choices using team capability, cost and interoperability.

sections.title: Fit before fashion
sections.body: Evaluate team size, skills, delivery speed, operational burden and compatibility with existing systems. A tool the team can operate well may outperform a more fashionable alternative.

sections.title: Look beyond the bill
sections.body: Total cost of ownership includes development, maintenance, training, data transfer and incident response. Tie spending to the business outcome and expected service levels.

sections.title: Cloud choices
sections.body: Hybrid cloud combines local and cloud environments; multicloud uses more than one cloud provider. Both can address constraints but add integration and governance work. Distinguish durable architectural principles from rapidly changing tools.

lessons.activity: Create a decision record comparing two storage options. State assumptions and a condition that would change your decision.

lessons.title: Write an architecture decision record
lessons.objective: Justify a storage and orchestration design with explicit trade-offs.

sections.title: State the workload
sections.body: A fictional retailer needs a daily sales report by 08:00 and a weekly model-training dataset. Begin with a batch design because the requirement does not call for sub-second data. Record volume, privacy constraints, failure tolerance and expected growth before selecting services.

sections.title: Choose and compare
sections.body: Compare an analytical warehouse with files in object storage plus a query engine. Consider schema evolution, query patterns, access control, operational effort and cost. A lake stores varied data; it still needs metadata, quality and lifecycle management to remain usable.

sections.title: Make the decision revisitable
sections.body: An architecture decision record captures context, options, decision, consequences and a review trigger. For orchestration, represent extract, validate, transform and publish as tasks with dependencies. Airflow represents workflows as directed acyclic graphs; task retries still require idempotent data operations.

lessons.activity: Write a one-page decision record for the retailer. Include a rejected option, an outage scenario and a trigger for reassessing the design.
lessons.code:
Context: daily report, ready by 08:00
Decision: scheduled batch ingestion
Quality gate: schema + keys + freshness
Recovery: retry the same partition safely
Review trigger: freshness needs fall below 5 minutes
lessons.codeCaption: Illustrative architecture decision outline, not a product recommendation.

quizzes.question: What belongs in total cost of ownership?
options: Development, operations and training as well as service costs
quizzes.explanation: Total cost of ownership accounts for the effort and expense of operating the system over its life.

quizzes.question: Why use a stable interface between services?
options: To reduce dependence on implementation details
quizzes.explanation: Stable interfaces can reduce coupling, although distributed systems still require coordination and operations.

quizzes.question: What should an architecture decision record include?
options: Context, alternatives, consequences and a review trigger
quizzes.explanation: A decision record makes the reasoning and conditions behind an architecture choice reviewable.

quizzes.question: What is a practical cost of introducing many microservices?
quizzes.explanation: Service boundaries may enable independence but also introduce network, observability and operational work.

quizzes.question: Which design directly acknowledges partial failure?
options: Timeouts, bounded retries and recovery paths
quizzes.explanation: Distributed components may fail independently; designs need explicit behavior for those failures.

quizzes.question: Hybrid cloud generally combines…
quizzes.explanation: Hybrid cloud connects on-premises or private infrastructure with public-cloud environments.

quizzes.question: Why consider team capability before choosing a tool?
options: Operating and maintaining it is part of the design cost
It removes the need for reliability
quizzes.explanation: A tool has to fit the skills and operational capacity of the people who will run it.

quizzes.question: What is a workflow DAG used to represent?
options: Dependencies between tasks without directed cycles
quizzes.explanation: A directed acyclic graph expresses task dependencies and valid ordering in a workflow.

quizzes.question: A data lake stores raw files. What is still needed?
options: Metadata, access control and quality management
A guarantee that every query is fast
quizzes.explanation: Storage alone does not make data understandable, trustworthy or appropriately accessible.

quizzes.question: A daily batch design must now support a five-second freshness target. What should the team do?
options: Revisit the architecture against the new requirement
quizzes.explanation: A changed service expectation is a reason to reassess the architecture and its trade-offs.

title: Make machine learning repeatable
name: MLOps & model development
description: Move from a promising experiment to a reproducible, risk-aware workflow.

lessons.title: Why MLOps exists
lessons.objective: Identify model lifecycle risks and the role of MLOps.

sections.title: More than a trained model
sections.body: A useful ML system needs data, code, runtime environments, evaluation and operational ownership. A good offline score alone does not establish production readiness.

sections.title: Recognize risk
sections.body: Risks include unreliable inputs, irreproducible experiments, inappropriate use and performance changes after deployment. Assess likelihood and impact, then define controls and owners.

sections.title: Responsible development
sections.body: Document intended use and limitations. Examine error patterns across relevant groups and use cases. Decide when a person must review a result or stop a deployment.

lessons.activity: Make a risk register for a house-price model with three risks, their impacts and proposed controls.

lessons.title: From objective to features
lessons.objective: Connect business objectives, exploration and feature selection.

sections.title: Define success first
sections.body: Translate a business question into a prediction target, an evaluation metric and an acceptable error range. Include a simple baseline so a complex model must justify its added effort.

sections.title: Explore before training
sections.body: Inspect missing values, outliers, distributions, time boundaries and target quality. Split data to reflect how future predictions will be made; keep evaluation data out of feature selection.

sections.title: Engineer with care
sections.body: Encoding, scaling, aggregation and domain-derived features can help. Avoid target leakage: a feature unavailable at prediction time can create misleading evaluation results.

lessons.activity: For churn prediction, propose three features available before the prediction date and one leakage feature to exclude.

lessons.title: Reproducible training & evaluation
lessons.objective: Record the inputs and artifacts required to repeat an experiment.

sections.title: An experiment is a record
sections.body: Track dataset version, code revision, dependency versions, parameters, random seeds and metrics. Store the resulting model artifact with the experiment that produced it.

sections.title: Compare appropriate baselines
sections.body: Select algorithms for the target, data and operational constraints. Compare with consistent splits and metrics. Accuracy alone may hide important error patterns on imbalanced data.

sections.title: Reproduction has limits
sections.body: Seeds help but may not guarantee bit-for-bit results across hardware and libraries. Document expected variability and verify that the relevant conclusions remain stable.

lessons.activity: Design an experiment log that another student could use to reproduce your baseline.

lessons.title: Track an experiment with MLflow
lessons.objective: Map experiment metadata to a minimal tracking workflow.

sections.title: Give each run an identity
sections.body: A run connects a candidate model to its parameters, metrics and artifacts. Choose an experiment name, record the code revision and dataset identifier, and log the evaluation metric. These records make comparisons reviewable; they do not guarantee that the underlying evaluation design is sound.

sections.title: Separate artifacts from numbers
sections.body: Metrics such as validation MAE describe measured behavior. Parameters record configuration. Artifacts include plots, feature lists, environment specifications and model files. Keep confidential data out of logs and restrict access to tracking storage.

sections.title: Use tracking with a good split
sections.body: Fit preprocessing on the training partition only, then apply it to validation data. MLflow can log an experiment, but it will not automatically prevent leakage in your feature construction. The minimal example below illustrates logging; it does not train or validate a real model.

lessons.activity: Design two comparable training runs. List what remains fixed, what changes and which artifacts a reviewer needs.
lessons.code:
import mlflow

mlflow.set_experiment("house-price-baseline")
with mlflow.start_run():
    mlflow.log_param("dataset_version", "demo-v1")
    mlflow.log_param("split_strategy", "time-based")
    mlflow.log_metric("validation_mae", 42000.0)
lessons.codeCaption: Illustrative logging example. The metric is fictional. Install and configure MLflow separately to run it.

quizzes.question: Which practice best supports reproducibility?
options: Recording data, code, environment and parameters
Renaming the model file each time
quizzes.explanation: Reproducing a run requires its inputs and environment, not just its final score.

quizzes.question: Which is an example of target leakage in churn prediction?
options: Account age before the prediction date
A cancellation flag recorded after the prediction date
Usage measured before the prediction date
quizzes.explanation: A future cancellation flag would not be available when making the intended prediction.

quizzes.question: When should a scaler learn its parameters?
options: From the combined training and test partitions
quizzes.explanation: Fit preprocessing on training data and reuse the learned transformation on held-out data.

quizzes.question: Why compare against a simple baseline?
options: To establish whether added complexity is useful
To guarantee the baseline is always best
quizzes.explanation: A baseline provides context for judging improvements and the cost of additional complexity.

quizzes.question: Which record is an experiment parameter?
options: A validation error measured after training
quizzes.explanation: Parameters describe configuration; metrics record measurements and artifacts store output files.

quizzes.question: Which record is an experiment artifact?
quizzes.explanation: Artifacts can include files such as plots, models and environment specifications.

quizzes.question: A model has 99% accuracy on a highly imbalanced dataset. What should you do?
options: Assume it is ready for production
Inspect class-specific metrics and error patterns
quizzes.explanation: Accuracy alone can hide poor performance on a small but important class.

quizzes.question: Do random seeds always guarantee identical results across hardware?
options: Yes, in every library and environment
No; document the environment and expected variability
quizzes.explanation: Hardware, libraries and nondeterministic operations can affect reproducibility despite fixed seeds.

quizzes.question: What is MLflow Tracking primarily useful for in an experiment?
options: Recording run metadata, metrics and artifacts
quizzes.explanation: Tracking makes run inputs and outputs reviewable, but evaluation design and operations remain your responsibility.

quizzes.question: Which is a sound model-development starting point?
options: Choose the largest model before defining the task
Define intended use, prediction target and evaluation criteria
quizzes.explanation: A clear objective and evaluation plan give the modeling work a meaningful target.

title: Ship with confidence
name: Production & CI/CD
description: Validate artifacts, automate delivery and plan a safe production release.

lessons.title: Prepare a production runtime
lessons.objective: Explain environment differences and model validation before launch.

sections.title: Development is not production
sections.body: Production has different traffic, permissions, dependencies and reliability expectations. Package the model and its runtime so behavior is consistent and configuration is explicit.

sections.title: Validate access and behavior
sections.body: Check input schemas, data access, dependencies and prediction interfaces before launch. Separate validation from the training process and test against the intended use.

sections.title: Evaluate model risk
sections.body: A higher-impact use case may need more review, documentation and monitoring. Decide release criteria before evaluating the candidate model, and record approval decisions.

lessons.activity: Write a pre-launch checklist covering environment, access, data schema and model behavior.

lessons.title: Build the CI/CD pipeline
lessons.objective: Design a delivery pipeline with meaningful quality gates.

sections.title: Continuous integration
sections.body: A code change triggers checks such as unit tests, schema validation and data-quality checks. Versioned artifacts connect each result to the source and environment that produced it.

sections.title: From candidate to release
sections.body: A pipeline can train, evaluate, package and validate a model before promoting it. Model metrics are one gate alongside security, interface and operational checks.

sections.title: Automate with judgment
sections.body: Continuous delivery keeps a validated candidate ready to release. Continuous deployment releases automatically after gates pass. Human approval may be appropriate depending on risk.

lessons.activity: Draw commit → test → train → evaluate → package → stage → approve → deploy. Add a stop condition to three stages.

lessons.title: Deployment & maintenance
lessons.objective: Compare deployment modes and plan rollback and maintenance.

sections.title: Match the serving pattern
sections.body: Batch prediction produces results on a schedule. Online prediction responds to requests. Select the mode using latency, throughput and business needs.

sections.title: Release gradually
sections.body: A canary release sends a small share of traffic to a new version. Blue-green uses parallel environments and a traffic switch. Shadow deployment evaluates a candidate without using its predictions for live decisions.

sections.title: Keep a recovery path
sections.body: Retain the last validated model and compatible environment. Monitor service health and model behavior, define rollback triggers and assign someone to respond.

lessons.activity: Plan a canary release. Define the traffic share, evaluation window, success criteria and rollback trigger.

lessons.title: Design release gates & a rollback record
lessons.objective: Specify evidence required to promote a candidate and recover safely.

sections.title: Make the candidate identifiable
sections.body: A release record links the model artifact, training dataset version, code commit, environment and evaluation report. Include the expected request schema and response contract. This allows a release to be investigated without guessing which model file was deployed.

sections.title: Separate kinds of tests
sections.body: Unit tests check transformation logic; data checks validate inputs; model checks evaluate quality; integration tests exercise prediction interfaces; load tests assess runtime behavior. A single accuracy threshold cannot substitute for these other checks. Compare the candidate with the deployed baseline under equivalent conditions.

sections.title: Rehearse recovery
sections.body: Before a canary, retain the last approved release and compatible configuration. Define who can stop the rollout, which metrics trigger rollback and how delayed labels affect the decision. Validate that the older model can still read the current input schema. A rollback that exists only on paper is not an operational plan.

lessons.activity: Draft a release record and three go/no-go gates. Add an owner, an observation window and a rollback decision for each.
lessons.code:
release: house-price-demo-v2
model: immutable-artifact-id
data: training-snapshot-id
code: source-commit-id
gates:
  - schema-compatible
  - evaluation-approved
  - latency-within-target
rollback: last-approved-release
lessons.codeCaption: Illustrative release record. Targets and approval rules depend on the application.

quizzes.question: What is the purpose of a release gate?
quizzes.explanation: Release gates prevent promotion until explicit quality and risk criteria are met.

quizzes.question: What is a canary release?
options: Sending a limited traffic share to a candidate version
Replacing every user request without observation
quizzes.explanation: A canary limits initial exposure so the candidate can be observed before expanding the rollout.

quizzes.question: What distinguishes shadow deployment?
options: Candidate predictions are evaluated without driving live decisions
quizzes.explanation: Shadow deployment observes a candidate alongside production without using its outputs for the live decision.

quizzes.question: A production runtime must include…
options: Compatible dependencies, configuration and prediction interfaces
quizzes.explanation: The model artifact needs a compatible environment and clear input/output expectations.

quizzes.question: What does continuous delivery emphasize?
options: A validated candidate kept ready for release
quizzes.explanation: Continuous delivery prepares validated changes for release; deployment may still require approval.

quizzes.question: What evidence belongs in a release record?
options: Model version, code revision, data version and evaluation report
quizzes.explanation: A release record connects the deployed artifact to the evidence and inputs that justify it.

quizzes.question: Which test checks that the prediction endpoint accepts the expected input?
quizzes.explanation: An interface test exercises the schema and behavior expected by clients of the prediction service.

quizzes.question: Why test rollback before a rollout?
options: To verify the earlier release remains compatible and recoverable
To avoid keeping the earlier artifact
To ensure the new model never needs monitoring
quizzes.explanation: Recovery depends on retained artifacts and compatibility, not just a written intention to roll back.

quizzes.question: Which serving mode suits a nightly list of predicted demand values?
options: No serving mode can support it
quizzes.explanation: Batch prediction fits results produced on a schedule when the business can wait for the batch.

quizzes.question: A model beats the baseline but exceeds the latency limit. Should it automatically pass?
options: Yes, quality scores override every requirement
No; operational requirements are also release gates
quizzes.explanation: Production readiness includes runtime constraints as well as model-quality criteria.

title: Keep models trustworthy
name: Monitoring & governance
description: Detect change, close the feedback loop and make model decisions traceable.

lessons.title: Recognize model degradation
lessons.objective: Distinguish input drift from changes in model performance.

sections.title: The world changes
sections.body: A model can degrade as customer behavior, products or data collection change. Monitor service health, input data and outcomes because each reveals a different class of problem.

sections.title: Drift is a signal
sections.body: Input drift means a feature distribution has changed relative to a reference. It does not prove prediction quality has declined. Investigate the cause and evaluate outcomes when labels are available.

sections.title: Use ground truth
sections.body: Ground-truth evaluation compares predictions with observed outcomes. Labels may arrive late, so define the evaluation window and distinguish early proxy signals from confirmed performance changes.

lessons.activity: For a demand forecast, list one service metric, one input-drift signal and one ground-truth metric.

lessons.title: Build the feedback loop
lessons.objective: Design monitoring and retraining decisions with validation.

sections.title: Choose a reference
sections.body: Compare recent inputs to a documented baseline. Missingness rates, summary statistics and distribution comparisons can highlight change; thresholds should reflect the use case and data variability.

sections.title: Investigate before reacting
sections.body: A drift alert could indicate real population change or a broken upstream transformation. Check data quality and context before retraining a model on potentially corrupted inputs.

sections.title: Retraining is another release
sections.body: Trigger retraining based on evidence or a schedule, then apply the same evaluation and release gates used for initial deployment. Keep an audit record and a rollback option.

lessons.activity: Write an alert playbook: trigger, owner, checks, decision and recovery. Include a reason not to retrain immediately.

lessons.title: Govern the model lifecycle
lessons.objective: Connect documentation and controls with model risk.

sections.title: Make ownership visible
sections.body: A model inventory records purpose, owner, versions, status and intended users. A model card adds evaluation results, data limitations and known failure modes.

sections.title: Scale controls with risk
sections.body: Use review, access control, lineage, approvals and change logs in proportion to the impact of model decisions. Reproducibility and traceability support responsible operations.

sections.title: Regulatory context
sections.body: Model governance includes risk management, privacy-aware data handling and clear accountability. Study how documentation, data handling and accountability relate to governance. Actual obligations depend on jurisdiction and context; this lesson is a conceptual introduction.

lessons.activity: Draft a model card with intended use, excluded uses, training data summary, evaluation, limitations and owner.

lessons.title: Write a monitoring incident playbook
lessons.objective: Turn an alert into an owned, evidence-based response.

sections.title: Begin with a concrete signal
sections.body: Suppose the missing-value rate for floor_area rises after a data-source change. An input alert is evidence of changed data, not proof of model failure. Inspect collection, schemas, transformations and affected traffic before acting. Record the baseline and the alert window.

sections.title: Separate diagnosis from retraining
sections.body: If a broken unit conversion caused the shift, repair the data path first. Retraining on corrupted inputs can reinforce the error. When labels arrive, compare outcome metrics and error slices against the baseline. Keep service failures, data drift and concept changes distinct in the investigation.

sections.title: Close the feedback loop
sections.body: Record the incident, impact, owner, corrective action and follow-up check. For any retraining decision, version the new data and reuse evaluation and release gates. Update the model card when intended use, limitations or measured behavior changes.

lessons.activity: Create a playbook for a sudden missing-feature alert. Include triage checks, an escalation owner and evidence required before retraining.
lessons.code:
Alert → acknowledge → inspect source
      → validate transformations
      → assess affected predictions
      → repair / rollback / evaluate retraining
      → validate recovery → record lessons
lessons.codeCaption: A conceptual response flow. Operational thresholds must be set for the actual system.

quizzes.question: An input-drift alert means…
options: The model must be retrained immediately
The input distribution changed and needs investigation
quizzes.explanation: Drift identifies a change in inputs; investigate data quality and outcome performance before deciding how to respond.

quizzes.question: Which observation directly measures model error when outcomes are available?
quizzes.explanation: Ground-truth evaluation measures predictive behavior against observed outcomes.

quizzes.question: A unit conversion bug changes a feature distribution. What should happen first?
options: Retrain immediately on the corrupted inputs
Investigate and repair the data transformation
quizzes.explanation: An upstream defect should be fixed before considering retraining on the changed data.

quizzes.question: What should a model card document?
options: Intended use, evaluation and known limitations
quizzes.explanation: Model cards support informed use by describing purpose, evaluation and constraints.

quizzes.question: Why can production accuracy be unavailable immediately?
options: Model versions remove the need for outcomes
quizzes.explanation: Many tasks have delayed ground truth, so early signals must be distinguished from confirmed outcome performance.

quizzes.question: What is a monitoring baseline?
options: A guarantee that drift is harmful
quizzes.explanation: A baseline defines the reference distribution or performance against which changes are assessed.

quizzes.question: Should a retrained model skip release validation?
options: Yes, retraining proves it is better
No, it should pass evaluation and release gates
Yes, if the data is newer
quizzes.explanation: New training data can introduce new failures; a retrained model needs evidence before promotion.

quizzes.question: How should governance effort relate to model risk?
options: Controls should reflect the impact and context of use
Every model needs identical controls regardless of impact
quizzes.explanation: Proportionate controls focus review and accountability where potential harm or failure matters most.

quizzes.question: Which belongs in an alert playbook?
options: An owner, diagnostic checks and escalation decisions
quizzes.explanation: An actionable playbook links a signal to accountable investigation and recovery decisions.

quizzes.question: A new customer population changes the relationship between features and outcomes. What concern does this suggest?
options: Possible concept drift requiring outcome-based evaluation
Proof that the network is unavailable
quizzes.explanation: A changed feature-to-outcome relationship suggests concept drift; evaluate behavior with suitable outcome evidence.
